claims.text: High-temperature mechanical softening in refractory high-entropy alloys is primarily caused by thermally activated migration and segregation of trace interstitial impurities.
Altered thermoelastic behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys is primarily caused by interstitial-impurity migration and segregation.
The initially cast Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is single-phase BCC.
The as-cast alloy has a uniform distribution of alloying elements and trace interstitials.
Oxygen and nitrogen interstitials initially provide solid-solution strengthening in Ti-V-Nb-Ta.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during thermal aging of Ti-V-Nb-Ta at 700°C.
At high temperature, interstitial impurities become mobile and form clusters or precipitates.
Impurity-driven segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the metal matrix.
Depletion of matrix interstitial solutes produces progressive mechanical softening with aging time.
Interstitial depletion alters the alloy's thermoelastic characteristics.
Impurity-doped Ti-V-Nb-Ta will undergo a larger aging-induced reduction in yield strength than a high-purity baseline.
Impurity-doped Ti-V-Nb-Ta will undergo a larger aging-induced reduction in elastic modulus than a high-purity baseline.
Microscopy of aged impurity-doped samples will reveal secondary phases or segregated regions relative to the high-purity baseline.
Minimizing impurities will suppress impurity-induced segregation and preserve a more uniform matrix.
The high-purity alloy will retain higher yield strength than the impurity-doped alloy at elevated temperature.
The high-purity alloy will have more stable thermoelastic behavior at elevated temperature.
The impurity-segregation mechanism applies over prolonged exposures from 700°C up to 1123 K.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that oxygen and nitrogen are initially solid-solution strengtheners, while the baseline asserts that minimizing those interstitials produces higher yield strength. A comparison of absolute strength therefore does not follow without specifying whether segregation removes enough strengthening in the doped alloy to make it weaker than the initially interstitial-poor control.
